A complete latent class analysis workflow with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/workflow-lca.Rmd
workflow-lca.Rmd

Latent class analysis (LCA) is a person-centred method for identifying unobserved subgroups in data measured on categorical indicators (Collins & Lanza, 2010). It assumes that the observations come from a small number of unobserved classes, each characterized by its own probability of every response to every indicator. Within a class, the indicators are assumed to be independent of one another; this assumption of local independence means that the classes alone account for the associations among the indicators. The model estimates the response probabilities of each class, the proportion of the sample in each class, and the posterior probability with which each observation belongs to each class.

In learning analytics, LCA has been used to identify the engagement state of each student in each course from indicators of online activity. In the VaSSTra method, these states are subsequently arranged into sequences across the courses of a programme, and similar sequences are grouped into trajectories of engagement (López-Pernas & Saqr, 2023, 2024). Saqr and López-Pernas (2021) and Saqr et al. (2023) applied this approach to the engagement of students followed through a complete study programme, so that the latent classes of single course enrolments form the building blocks of students’ longitudinal trajectories.

As with latent profile analysis, an LCA involves a sequence of decisions: the number of classes, the estimation from multiple starting values, the interpretation of the classes, the evaluation of the classification and of local independence, and the relation of the classes to other variables (Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Weller et al., 2020). This vignette presents a complete single-level analysis in that order and extends the model to two levels in the final section. In the output of this package the classes of observations are labelled profile_1, profile_2, and so on.

library(latents)
set.seed(1)

The estimation uses random starting values; the seed is therefore set once so that the results can be reproduced.

Data

The student_esm data contain 2,582 experience-sampling reports from 100 university students, collected in a study of academic adjustment (Neubauer & Schmiedek, 2024). At each report made when they had not studied since the previous prompt, a student indicated whether they had been engaged in each of eight activities since the previous report, and rated how happy, relaxed, worried and exhausted they felt. The aim of the analysis is to identify typical combinations of activities.

activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
summary(subset(student_esm, select = activities))
#>  time_with_friends on_social_media tv_video_games listened_music sports     walking   
#>  no :2211          no :1837        no :2033       no :2193       no :2397   no :2254  
#>  yes: 371          yes: 745        yes: 549       yes: 389       yes: 185   yes: 328  
#>  reading    part_time_job
#>  no :2291   no :2479     
#>  yes: 291   yes: 103

Every activity is absent at most reports. Social media is the most frequent (745 reports) and a part-time job the least frequent (103), so the classes are distinguished by how far their probabilities of each activity exceed these base rates.

The reports are nested in students. The first part of this vignette treats each report as an independent observation, which corresponds to the conventional single-level model; the nesting is taken into account in the final section.

Selecting the number of classes

The number of classes is not estimated by the model but specified by the analyst, and is therefore chosen by fitting models with different numbers of classes and comparing them (see the class enumeration article). enumerate_lca() estimates models with one to six classes and returns the results in one table.

models <- enumerate_lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 1:6)
#> 2 of 6 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (classes4, classes5); refit those you consider with more starts.
plot_enumeration(models)

summary(models)
#> Class enumeration: 6 candidates, 6 converged, 0 failed to fit
#> 3 distinct candidate(s) are minimal under some criterion.
#> No candidate is selected automatically. Choose one convention and keep it.
#> 
#> ! 2 of 6 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only
#>     (classes4, classes5); refit those you consider with more starts.
#> ! 5 candidates have a class with average posterior below 0.8 (classes2,
#>     classes3, classes4, classes5, classes6).
#> 
#> -- lowest value of each criterion --------------------------------
#>  criterion  convention candidate value
#>        aic        <NA>  classes6 15648
#>        kic        <NA>  classes6 15704
#>        bic      groups  classes4 15888
#>        bic individuals  classes4 15888
#>      sabic      groups  classes4 15777
#>      sabic individuals  classes4 15777
#>       caic      groups  classes4 15923
#>       caic individuals  classes4 15923
#>        awe      groups  classes1 16220
#>        awe individuals  classes1 16220
#>        icl      groups  classes1 16133
#>        icl individuals  classes1 16133
#>        clc      groups  classes1 16070
#>        clc individuals  classes1 16070
#> 
#> -- knees of bic_groups ----------------------------------------
#>   direction           line knee_candidate knee_without_largest stable
#>    profiles  1 group class       classes2             classes2   TRUE
#>  parameters all candidates       classes2             classes2   TRUE
#> 
#> Tables: get_candidates(x), get_best(x), get_deltas(x), get_knees(x),
#>         get_tree(x), get_classification(x), get_entropy(x), get_checks(x).
#> Plots:  plot_criteria(x), plot_deltas(x), plot_avepp(x), plot_tree(x), plot_all(x).

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) is lowest for four classes, 13.2 points below the three-class model. The fourth class, however, contains 1.3% of the reports (about 32), which describe many activities at once, and the four-class model reaches its best log likelihood from only one of its starting values. A class of this size, supported by a solution that the starts do not replicate, is weakly supported, and the ICL (Biernacki et al., 2000), which additionally penalizes classification uncertainty, is lower for three classes than for four. The ICL is lowest for one class, which has no uncertainty to penalize, and among the models with more than one class it is lowest for two; the two-class solution, however, has a relative entropy below 0.5 and therefore separates the reports poorly. The three-class model is retained.

Estimation

lca() fits a single-level latent class model, estimated by maximum likelihood with the expectation-maximization algorithm from multiple starting values.

fit <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3)
fit
#> Latent class analysis: 3 classes
#> 2582 observations; 8 categorical indicators
#> Classes are labelled profile_1, profile_2, ... in every table.
#> Log likelihood: -7848.453248 | AIC: 15748.906 | BIC: 15901.171
#> Converged: TRUE | iterations: 39 | best log likelihood reached by 2 of 10 starts (10 converged)
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 3.6% (94)   profile_2 57.7% (1490)   profile_3 38.7% (999)
#> 
#> Response probabilities
#>          indicator category profile_1 profile_2 profile_3

#>    on_social_media       no     0.955     0.503     1.000

Interpretation of the classes

The heatmap shows, for each class, the estimated probability that the activity was reported.

plot_profiles(fit, what = "heatmap")

The largest class, comprising 58% of the reports, is characterized by screen-based activities: social media, television and video games, and music. The smallest class, 4% of the reports, consists almost entirely of reports of working at a part-time job. The third class, 39% of the reports, has elevated probabilities of spending time with friends, walking and sport, and a probability of social media use close to zero. The same probabilities are shown below as profiles across the activities, with 95% confidence intervals where the probability is not on its boundary.

plot_responses(fit)
#> Warning: The fitted likelihood still carries a score worth 1.6% of a standard error;
#> refit with a tighter `tol` before using Wald inference.

The probabilities with their standard errors. Several are estimated at zero or one; a standard error is not defined on the boundary of the parameter space, so those are held at their bound and have none.

head(get_results(fit, "responses"), 8)
#> Warning: The fitted likelihood still carries a score worth 1.6% of a standard error;
#> refit with a tighter `tol` before using Wald inference.
#>   profile         indicator category probability threshold probability_standard_error
#> 1       1 time_with_friends       no      0.9807    3.9263                    0.01497
#> 2       2 time_with_friends       no      0.9050    2.2543                    0.00945
#> 3       3 time_with_friends       no      0.7720    1.2198                    0.02004
#> 4       1 time_with_friends      yes      0.0193        NA                    0.01497
#> 5       2 time_with_friends      yes      0.0950        NA                    0.00945
#> 6       3 time_with_friends      yes      0.2280        NA                    0.02004
#> 7       1   on_social_media       no      0.9550    3.0547                    0.03352
#> 8       2   on_social_media       no      0.5027    0.0108                    0.03788

Classification quality

diagnostics() reports the classification measures and draws the four classification plots: the effective size of each class, the distribution of the posterior probability of each report’s assigned class, each report’s contribution to the classification entropy, and the average posterior probability matrix, which shows which classes are confused with which.

diagnostics(fit)

#> Diagnostics: Latent class analysis, 3 classes
#> 2 checks need attention: estimates at a bound; pairs dependent within a class
#> 
#> Estimation
#>   ok     best start converged                                yes                      
#>   info   best log likelihood reached by                      2 of 10 starts           
#>   ok     starts failed or unfinished                         0 of 10                  
#>   check  estimates at a bound                                yes                      
#>          a variance, probability, count mean or dispersion is at a numerical bound; ordinary Wald inference may be unavailable
#> 
#> Class size
#>   info   smallest class                         individuals  3.6% (n = 94, class 1)   
#>   info   modal vs estimated proportions         individuals  largest gap 0.120        
#>   ok     classes with no assigned unit          individuals  0 of 3                   
#> 
#> Classification
#>   info   relative entropy                       individuals  0.662                    
#>   info   lowest average posterior               individuals  0.705 (class 3)          
#>   info   lowest odds of correct classification  individuals  3.8 (class 3)            
#> 
#> Local independence
#>   check  pairs dependent within a class                      4 of 84 tested pairs     BH-adjusted p < 0.05
#>          smallest adjusted p: listened_music x walking in profile_2, residual 0.110, adjusted p 0.0019
#> 
#> Information
#>   info   log likelihood, parameters, BIC                     -7848.45, 26, 15901.17   
#> 
#> Every check with its reference: get_results(x, "checks"). Other tables: get_results(x, what = ).

The relative entropy of 0.66 (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) indicates a moderately clear classification, although the reports of the third class are assigned with an average posterior of only 0.71. Relative entropy describes the quality of the classification for the chosen model rather than serving as a criterion for the number of classes (Sorgente et al., 2025).

Local dependence

The latent class model assumes that the activities are independent within each class. The bivariate residual of a pair of activities compares their observed co-occurrence within a class with the co-occurrence the model implies, and a large value indicates a dependence the classes do not explain. The p-value refers this Pearson statistic to a chi-square distribution that ignores the estimation of the model’s table, which makes it very conservative: in one simulation from a correctly specified two-class model (n = 500, 200 replications) it rejected 0.25% of pairs per class, and 0.08% pooled, at a nominal 5%. p_adjusted is corrected across all the pairs by Benjamini-Hochberg (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). A pair that passes the filter below is therefore strong evidence of dependence, but a pair that does not pass it is not evidence of independence.

subset(get_results(fit, "residuals"), p_adjusted < 0.01)
#>     profile    indicator_1 indicator_2        kind observed expected residual effective_n
#> 3 profile_2 listened_music     walking categorical     0.11 4.24e-17     0.11        1490
#>   statistic df  p_value p_adjusted
#> 3        18  1 2.23e-05    0.00187

The largest residual is that of listening to music and walking in class 2 (18). local_dependence names pairs of categorical indicators that are modelled jointly within each class: the pair then has its own joint distribution in every class, and the other activities remain independent given the class.

dependent <- lca(student_esm, activities, n_classes = 3,
                 local_dependence = "listened_music:walking")
get_results(dependent, "local_dependence")
#>                      pair        kind profile         item_1 category_1  item_2
#> 1  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music         no walking
#> 2  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music         no walking
#> 3  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music        yes walking
#> 4  listened_music:walking categorical       1 listened_music        yes walking
#> 5  listened_music:walking categorical       2 listened_music         no walking
#> 6  listened_music:walking categorical       2 listened_music         no walking
#> 7  listened_music:walking categorical       2 listened_music        yes walking
#> 8  listened_music:walking categorical       2 listened_music        yes walking
#> 9  listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music         no walking
#> 10 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music         no walking
#> 11 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music        yes walking
#> 12 listened_music:walking categorical       3 listened_music        yes walking
#>    category_2 probability independent    ratio covariance correlation
#> 1          no    7.66e-01    0.761730 1.01e+00         NA          NA
#> 2         yes    2.18e-01    0.222601 9.79e-01         NA          NA
#> 3          no    7.49e-03    0.012125 6.18e-01         NA          NA
#> 4         yes    8.18e-03    0.003543 2.31e+00         NA          NA
#> 5          no    9.37e-01    0.937446 9.99e-01         NA          NA
#> 6         yes    4.75e-02    0.046722 1.02e+00         NA          NA
#> 7          no    1.58e-02    0.015080 1.05e+00         NA          NA
#> 8         yes    1.00e-10    0.000752 1.33e-07         NA          NA
#> 9          no    7.20e-01    0.703997 1.02e+00         NA          NA
#> 10        yes    3.81e-02    0.053593 7.10e-01         NA          NA
#> 11         no    2.10e-01    0.225262 9.31e-01         NA          NA
#> 12        yes    3.27e-02    0.017148 1.91e+00         NA          NA

The table gives each class’s joint probabilities of the pair beside the products of its marginal probabilities, which are the probabilities under independence, and their ratio. The two models describe the same data and are compared with compare_models().

compare_models(independent = fit, dependent = dependent)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model        Classes   k    LogLik       BIC  ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8
#> -----------  -------  --  --------  --------  ----  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----
#> independent        3  26  -7848.45  15901.17  0.00   0.561  17820.27     0.66       0.71      1
#> dependent          3  29  -7836.91  15901.66  0.49   0.439  17816.33     0.66       0.70      1

The joint model raises the log likelihood by 11.5 at the cost of 3 parameters, and BIC is lower for the independent model. The dependence is present in the data, and the three classes describe the activities about as well without modelling it.

Classes and a distal outcome

three_step() estimates the mean of an outcome within each class. It uses the BCH method, which applies the inverse estimated classification-error matrix to modal class assignments (Bolck et al., 2004). These corrected weights can be negative; posterior-probability weighting is the separate method = "proportional" option. The outcome here is the happiness rating.

happiness <- three_step(fit, student_esm, outcome = "happy")
happiness
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class  Mean        95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  ----  ------------  -----  -----------
#>     1  4.53  [4.22, 4.83]  0.156        88.80
#>     2  4.63  [4.53, 4.73]  0.051       957.30
#>     3  5.30  [5.16, 5.43]  0.068       549.14

Happiness is highest in the class of reports away from screens (5.30 on the seven-point scale), and lower in the screen-based class (4.63) and the work class (4.53).

Extension to two levels

Each student contributes many reports, so the reports are not independent. When the student identifier is supplied as id, multilca() estimates a two-level model: the classes of reports are estimated again, jointly with the student classes, and need not coincide with the single-level classes; the students are in addition grouped into latent classes that differ in the proportion of their reports belonging to each class.

two_level <- multilca(student_esm, activities, id = "student",
                      n_profiles = 3, n_group_classes = 2)
get_results(two_level, "profile_probabilities")
#>   group_class profile probability group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1      0.2264                    0.36
#> 2           1       2      0.1052                    0.36
#> 3           1       3      0.6685                    0.36
#> 4           2       1      0.2513                    0.64
#> 5           2       2      0.7271                    0.64
#> 6           2       3      0.0216                    0.64

The two-level model is presented in detail in vignette("lca").
